title: Turn risk into secure requirements and design: decision comparison 1
teachingQuestion: How does a product risk become a testable security/privacy requirement, a design decision, and acceptance evidence?
focalInsight: IPT decision, security/privacy outcomes, threat boundary, control assumption, acceptance criterion, and change-triggered review.
caption: Compare meaning, decision conditions, and failures. These concise distinctions are paired with the worked examples in the teaching unit.

nodes.label: Security Requirements
nodes.definition: Observable security outcomes or constraints the system must satisfy, such as authorized access, integrity protection, auditable events, or safe failure.
nodes.decision: Write each requirement with context, owner, measurable acceptance evidence, and any approved exception before selecting implementation.
nodes.failureExample: “Use encryption” without scope, key authority, and a test leaves confidentiality behavior ambiguous.
nodes.detail: Observable security outcomes or constraints the system must satisfy, such as authorized access, integrity protection, auditable events, or safe failure.

nodes.label: Privacy Requirements
nodes.definition: Requirements governing lawful and appropriate collection, use, disclosure, retention, access, and deletion of personal data in the product.
nodes.decision: Identify data purpose and lifecycle with privacy stakeholders, then define constraints and evidence for the affected flow.
nodes.failureExample: A feature can meet functional needs while retaining personal data longer or sharing it more broadly than allowed.
nodes.detail: Requirements governing lawful and appropriate collection, use, disclosure, retention, access, and deletion of personal data in the product.

nodes.label: Threat Modeling
nodes.definition: Structured analysis of assets, actors, trust boundaries, entry points, abuse cases, and control assumptions from an attacker perspective.
nodes.decision: Perform and update it when architecture, data flow, exposure, or key assumptions change; use results to choose controls and tests.
nodes.failureExample: Reusing a model after adding an external queue misses the new boundary and abuse paths.
nodes.detail: Structured analysis of assets, actors, trust boundaries, entry points, abuse cases, and control assumptions from an attacker perspective.

nodes.label: Secure Design
nodes.definition: Architecture and detailed design that deliberately enforces requirements through boundaries, authorization, validation, isolation, cryptography, logging, and resilient behavior.
nodes.decision: Choose a control because it mitigates a modeled abuse case and document its dependencies, failure behavior, and verification.
nodes.failureExample: Adding authentication without authorization can still let a valid low-privilege user initiate refunds.
nodes.detail: Architecture and detailed design that deliberately enforces requirements through boundaries, authorization, validation, isolation, cryptography, logging, and resilient behavior.

nodes.label: Integrated Product Team
nodes.definition: A cross-functional group that makes product tradeoffs with product, engineering, security, privacy, operations, legal, and relevant users/partners.
nodes.decision: Use the IPT early to resolve conflicting requirements and assign owners for decisions that cross disciplines.
nodes.failureExample: A security team discovering a retention constraint after release may require costly redesign or unlawful processing.
nodes.detail: A cross-functional group that makes product tradeoffs with product, engineering, security, privacy, operations, legal, and relevant users/partners.

nodes.label: Acceptance Criteria
nodes.definition: Pre-agreed, observable conditions and evidence used to decide whether a delivered system meets its specified requirements.
nodes.decision: Make criteria trace to the requirement and abuse case; test normal, failure, and misuse behavior before acceptance or explicit risk disposition.
nodes.failureExample: A login test that proves only a valid user can sign in does not prove invalid signatures or unauthorized roles are rejected.
nodes.detail: Pre-agreed, observable conditions and evidence used to decide whether a delivered system meets its specified requirements.

learningContract.teachingQuestion: How does a product risk become a testable security/privacy requirement, a design decision, and acceptance evidence?
learningContract.misconception: Naming encryption or authentication is a complete security requirement, and a threat model is a one-time document.
learningContract.formRationale: Aligned columns make concept meanings, decision criteria and failure consequences explicit and comparable.
learningContract.focalInsight: IPT decision, security/privacy outcomes, threat boundary, control assumption, acceptance criterion, and change-triggered review.
learningContract.intentionalOmissions: Do not prescribe a single threat-model method, encryption algorithm, privacy law, or approval workflow.
learningContract.retrievalPrompt: A new partner webhook can initiate refunds. State one abuse case, one testable requirement, one design control, and one acceptance test.
